strengths: The RAD framework is clearly specified: the five-step pipeline (retrieve, rerank, extract, classify, vote) is formalized with explicit equations, database construction is described, and implementation details (encoder, retrieval size K=50, reranking size k=10, defender LLM, judge models, prompts in Appendix C) support reproducibility.

The safety-utility trade-off evaluation via operating curves under an explicit FRR budget is a genuinely useful contribution; it frames defense deployment more practically than single-threshold reporting and is a scheme others could adopt.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: three target models, four attack families (PAIR, PAP, template, DAN), comparisons against three prior defenses (Self-Reminder, Llama Guard 3, Intention Analysis), 95% confidence intervals over seeds for template attacks, and ablation-style studies of both adding new attack examples (Section 4.4.1) and scaling the database to 500k examples (Section 4.4.2).

The training-free adaptability claim is directly tested: Figure 3 shows improved defense when PAP examples are added, and Figure 4 shows stable performance against previously seen attacks as the database grows to 500k entries.
Ethical considerations are addressed thoughtfully, including restricted access to the jailbreak database, content warnings, dataset usage statements, and an AI-assistance disclosure.
weaknesses: The core defense evaluation is largely in-distribution: Section 4.2 explicitly evaluates 'attacks whose examples are already in the database.' The main claim of strong defense against PAP and PAIR thus substantially reflects retrieval of same-family examples, which weakens the headline claim of general jailbreak prevention. Only the DAN template split and the PAP add/remove study probe generalization; there is no systematic unseen-attack or adaptive-attacker evaluation, which is the standard stress test for defenses in this area.

Novelty is moderate. Retrieval-based jailbreak defenses already exist (RePD, EDDF, cited by the authors), and the extract step is acknowledged to be conceptually equivalent to prior Intention Analysis work; the combination with majority voting and the FRR-budget evaluation is incremental over these.

Inference cost and latency are a practical concern that is under-discussed: the pipeline makes roughly k+1 (~11) LLM calls per query plus embedding retrieval, with a reported ~30 seconds per case. Against lightweight alternatives like Llama Guard, the cost-benefit trade-off deserves explicit analysis, especially given the modest margins over Intention Analysis on some settings.

Some design choices and results lack analysis or ablation: why k=10 and K=50, no ablation isolating the contribution of the reranking step, extraction step, or voting scheme, and RAD underperforms Intention Analysis on PAIR-1 and PAP for GPT-4o-mini (rows 9 vs. 10-11) without discussion.

The benign query set (313 GPT-4o-synthesized queries) is small and synthetic, so FRR estimates carry uncertainty; harmfulness definition is tied entirely to StrongREJECT labels, which the authors acknowledge.

Reproducibility is asserted ('link to the source code is provided in the Abstract') but no code or database access is actually available at review time; the restricted-access database policy also limits external verification of the central component.
Writing has minor issues (e.g., duplicated 'The The' in Section 3.2, 'Thirteen' typos in references), and Figure 1 is dense enough to require careful reading.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem—adaptable jailbreak defense—and clearly motivates two concrete desiderata (training-free updatability and controllable safety-utility trade-off).

The FRR-budget operating-curve evaluation is a sensible and somewhat fresh framing: reporting defense performance under an explicit false-refusal budget is more deployment-relevant than single-threshold comparisons, and Figure 2/3 use it consistently.

Experimental coverage is reasonably broad: three target models, four attack families (PAIR, PAP, template, DAN), and comparisons against three prior defenses including a strong guard model (Llama Guard 3).

The paper is largely self-critical about scope: it openly notes that main-table results are for 'seen' attacks, includes a generalization check across attack variants (PAIR-1 vs PAIR-5), a database-scaling study (Section 4.4), and appendices with prompts, judge details, and runtime—supporting reproducibility.
Ethical considerations, intended use, and dataset usage are addressed, and the harm taxonomy of the examples is handled with appropriate care.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is largely in-distribution: Section 4.2 explicitly evaluates 'attacks whose examples are already added to the database.' The headline claim of 'strong defense' therefore mostly demonstrates retrieval of near-duplicate attacks, which inflates apparent effectiveness. There is no held-out evaluation against a genuinely novel attack family absent from the database, and no adaptive-attacker analysis (e.g., paraphrasing or deliberately off-database strategies), which is standard expectation for defense papers.

Novelty is limited. The authors themselves position RAD against RePD and EDDF, which also use retrieval for jailbreak defense; RAD is essentially RAG-style nearest-neighbor lookup plus intent extraction plus ensemble voting over an off-the-shelf LLM. The pipeline is a plausible engineering combination rather than a new insight, and the paper does not isolate which component drives the gains.

The aggregation math is questionable. Equation (10) sums joint probabilities across k+1 retrieved strategies; these are not guaranteed to be calibrated or to sum to at most 1, and no calibration analysis is provided. The claimed probabilistic interpretation (Eq. 9) is heuristic at best.

The benign query set is synthetic (GPT-4o-generated counterparts of StrongREJECT harmful queries, reviewed by the authors). FRR measured on such near-paraphrase benign queries may not reflect real-world benign traffic distribution, so the safety-utility trade-off conclusions may be optimistic; no external benign benchmark (e.g., MT/production queries) is used.

Latency and cost are a serious deployment concern that the paper underplays: ~30 seconds per query with 10+ LLM calls per classification (K=10 reranked candidates each requiring extraction and classification). A defense slower than the target model's own generation is of questionable practical value, yet this is not analyzed against baselines' cost.

Statistical rigor is uneven: 5-seed confidence intervals are reported only for DAN; PAIR/PAP/template numbers have no reported variance, and single-run GPT-generated attack prompts introduce additional unquantified noise.

The 500k-example scaling experiment is only sketched—how the 500k DAN examples were generated/validated is unclear, and 'curves remain flat' is presented without analysis of retrieval quality degradation at scale.
Reproducibility claim is inconsistent: the Ethical Statement says a code link is 'provided in the Abstract,' but no link appears there. Restricted-access data also limits independent verification.
Comparison fairness is unclear: RAD uses a 14B defender model while Llama Guard 3 is a much smaller guard model; parameter/compute-matched comparisons and ablations over defender size are absent.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem—adaptable jailbreak defense—with a clear motivation for training-free updates and controllable safety-utility trade-offs, both well-articulated as central challenges

The proposed RAD pipeline (retrieve, rerank, extract, classify, vote) is clearly formalized with explicit notation, and the database construction and inference steps are described in enough detail to understand the method

Experiments cover three target models (Qwen-2.5-14B, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B), multiple attack families (PAIR, PAP, template-based, DAN), and reasonable baselines (Self-Reminder, Llama Guard 3, Intention Analysis)

The proposed FRR-budget operating-curve evaluation is a sensible and practitioner-relevant contribution that goes beyond single-point comparisons, and the Pareto-style analysis in Figures 2-3 is informative
The database-scaling experiments (Section 4.4.2, up to 500K added examples) directly test a realistic deployment concern and support the claim that performance is invariant to database size

Good reproducibility support: implementation details, model versions, prompts, refusal-judge prompt, and runtime information are provided in the appendix; ethical risks of releasing jailbreak databases are discussed
The paper is generally well written and organized, with a clear system overview in Figure 1
weaknesses: The evaluation is largely circular with respect to the threat model: all attack families tested (PAIR, PAP, templates, DAN) have examples in the database, so the headline results measure defense against seen attack families rather than generalization to novel or adaptive attacks; no unseen-attack or adaptive-attacker experiment is reported

The benign query set is only 313 queries synthesized by GPT-4o from the harmful StrongREJECT queries; FRR estimates on this small, synthetic, topically matched distribution may not reflect real-world benign traffic, weakening the safety-utility trade-off claims
Evaluation relies on GPT-4o-mini as the judge for both attack success and false refusals, introducing potential judge bias; no human validation of judge reliability is reported
The defender model (Qwen-2.5-14B) is also one of the target models, and classification uses its logits; potential overlap/confounding effects between defender and target are not discussed or ablated

Baseline tuning appears uneven: e.g., Intention Analysis shows an 18.85% FRR on GPT-4o-mini, raising questions about whether prior systems were given comparable care in threshold/configuration selection
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for the main Table 1 results (CIs appear only for DAN)

Novelty is moderate: retrieval-based jailbreak defenses (RePD, EDDF) already exist, and RAD is best viewed as an incremental combination of known ideas (retrieval, intent inversion akin to Intention Analysis, ensembling) with a new evaluation protocol

The claimed code link is said to be 'provided in the Abstract' but no link actually appears in the submitted manuscript, which hurts verifiability; the >500K-example database construction is also underspecified for the main experiments

Efficiency is barely addressed: the multi-step pipeline (50 retrievals, extraction and classification per retrieved example) is costly, and the reported ~30 seconds per case is not broken down or compared against baselines

strengths: The core design—treating jailbreak defense as retrieval-augmented detection with a training-free, updatable database of attack examples—directly addresses a genuine practical need (rapid adaptation to new attack strategies), and is well-motivated by the adaptability and controllability challenges articulated in the introduction.

The experimental evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: three target models, six attack methods spanning multiple families and years (2023–2025), four baseline defenses (Self-Reminder, Llama Guard 3, Intention Analysis, SCR) with carefully matched database/retriever settings for SCR, an incremental database-expansion study demonstrating adaptation without catastrophic forgetting, scaling experiments up to 500k examples, per-step latency analysis, and component ablations (reranking and voting strategies).

The proposed FRR-budget/operating-curve evaluation scheme is a genuinely useful methodological contribution: it moves beyond single operating-point comparisons and gives practitioners a principled way to deploy defenses under a false-refusal constraint, and it exposes trade-offs (e.g., IA's high FRR on GPT-4o-mini) that fixed-threshold comparisons obscure.

Utility preservation is evaluated on both free-form (AlpacaEval 2.0) and multiple-choice (MMLU) benchmarks, showing RAD avoids the substantial utility degradation seen in prompt-modification baselines—an important and often-neglected dimension.

Reproducibility support is strong: implementation details (models, prompts, libraries, seeds, confidence intervals), database entry examples, judge prompts, and a code/data release are provided; the ethical statement and access restrictions for the attack database are appropriate.
weaknesses: Novelty over prior RAG-based defenses (RePD, SCR, EDDF) is incremental. The individual components—dense retrieval, LLM-based strategy inference and query extraction, ensemble classification, threshold tuning—are largely known techniques; the paper's differentiation (tunable threshold, detection rather than response modification, continual database updates) is argued qualitatively (Appendix G) more than demonstrated against these baselines head-to-head on the adaptation axis.

Evaluation against unseen attacks is confined to attack families with known templates; examples in the database are drawn from the same families as the evaluation attacks (with template splits). Robustness to genuinely out-of-distribution or obfuscated attacks (e.g., cipher/encoding-based, multilingual) is not tested, and no adaptive-attacker experiment (attacker aware of RAD) is included, which limits claims about real-world robustness.

The false-refusal evaluation relies on only 313 synthetic benign queries generated by GPT-4o and reviewed by the authors. These are constructed to closely mirror the harmful StrongREJECT queries, so reported FRRs may underestimate false refusals on natural, diverse benign traffic; no established benign benchmark (e.g., OR-Bench, WildTeaming benign subset, XSTest) is used.

All main results use a single safety benchmark (StrongREJECT, 313 harmful queries) and GPT-based judge models, raising concerns about evaluation-set breadth and potential judge bias (the defender LLM is Qwen while judges are GPT models; a separate GPT-4 judge decides false refusal).

Deployment cost is nontrivial: even optimized, the pipeline costs ~7.5s per query dominated by the extraction step requiring multiple LLM generations (k=10 per query), and this is only addressed in the appendix; the practical viability relative to single-pass guards (Llama Guard) deserves main-text treatment.

Several design choices are under-analyzed: sensitivity to retrieval quality, behavior when the extractor LLM fails to invert a transformation, and how performance degrades as the query/strategy distribution drifts far from the database, are only touched on indirectly.

strengths: The core claim—that a retrieval-augmented detector enables training-free adaptation to newly discovered jailbreak strategies—is clearly formulated and directly tested: the incremental database-expansion experiment (Table 2) provides concrete evidence that adding examples of new attacks (ReNeLLM, SATA) improves defense on those attacks without degrading performance on previously covered attacks.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: three target models, six attack methods spanning template-based and adaptive LLM-driven attacks (PAIR, PAP, DAN, ReNeLLM, SATA), ablations of reranking and voting components (Table 7), non-GPT attacker families (Table 5), latency analysis (Table 6), and database scaling to 500k examples (Table 8, Figure 4).

The proposed FRR-budget operating-curve evaluation is a genuine methodological contribution: it exposes the fixed, uncontrollable operating points of prior defenses (e.g., IA and SCR's high FRR on GPT-4o-mini in Table 1) and makes the safety-utility trade-off comparable across systems, which prior RAG-based defenses (RePD, EDDF, SCR) did not do.

The utility-preservation experiments on AlpacaEval 2.0 and MMLU (Table 3) appropriately test for collateral damage on benign behavior, showing RAD as a detection system preserves utility where prompt-modifying defenses degrade it.

Reproducibility is well supported: implementation details (models, K/k values, prompts, seed handling, 95% CIs) are extensive across Appendices C–E, code and data are stated to be released, and the attacker implementations follow established benchmark settings.
weaknesses: The core mechanism has limited novelty relative to closely related prior work—RePD (retrieves jailbreak examples for decomposition), EDDF (retrieves attack strategies), and SCR (rapidly incorporates newly identified jailbreaks into a retrieval pool). RAD's distinctives are the explicit decision threshold and ensemble classification with PMI reranking, which feel incremental; the paper's positioning in Appendix G is argumentative rather than empirically differentiating against RePD/EDDF at scale.

Evaluation relies heavily on GPT-family models in overlapping roles: GPT-4o-mini generates attacks, judges StrongREJECT attack success, and the benign set is synthesized with GPT-4o from the same harmful queries. This circularity risks systematically favorable attack scores/judgments, and the 313 self-reviewed synthetic benign queries are a narrow proxy for real-world benign traffic (no natural user queries, multilingual, or edge-case benign content), so the low FRR claims rest on a small, author-constructed set.

Unseen-attack generalization is weaker than the framing suggests: RAD fundamentally depends on similarity between the input and stored attack examples. Attacks using genuinely novel obfuscation far from any database entry may evade retrieval, and the paper does not evaluate any attack type that is stylistically distant from everything in the database; the 'adaptability' claim is really a nearest-neighbor generalization claim.

Strong adaptive attacks remain insufficiently defended: PAIR-5 scores stay at ~40–49 for RAD vs. ~59–90 undefended, and the pairing of RAD with Llama-3.1-8B (which exhibits ≥2.5% inherent FRR) shows detection thresholds cannot fix refusals baked into the target model.

Practical deployment cost is underplayed in the main text: the defender requires an LLM extraction step costing 7.5–22 seconds per prompt even with vLLM optimization, which is substantial for production traffic filtering, and this appears only in an appendix.

Table 1 reports RAD at a single fixed threshold (0.5) against baselines at their fixed operating points; while Figure 2 partially mitigates this, per-cell comparisons in the main table do not equalize FRR across systems, making some 'best' claims ambiguous.

strengths: Clear problem framing around two practical challenges—adaptability to emerging attacks and controllable safety-utility trade-offs—which motivates the design and the evaluation protocol well.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three target models (Qwen-2.5-14B, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B), multiple attack families (PAIR, PAP, Template, DAN, ReNeLLM, SATA), several baselines (Self-Reminder, Llama Guard 3, IA, SCR), non-GPT attackers, and component ablations (reranking/voting schemes).

The FRR-budget operating-curve evaluation (Section 3.4, Figure 2) is a genuinely useful contribution: it makes safety-utility trade-offs explicit and comparable across defenses with a single fixed operating point, and the finding that Llama-3.1-8B has a floor on achievable FRR is insightful.

The incremental database-expansion study (Table 2) directly tests the central adaptability claim, showing improvement on newly added attacks (yellow-to-blue diagonal) without degradation on previously seen attacks; the 500k-example scaling analysis (Appendix M) further supports deployment stability.

Strong utility preservation results (Table 3): RAD matches the undefended model on AlpacaEval 2.0 and MMLU, whereas IA and SCR cause large degradation—a meaningful practical advantage of detection-style defenses.

Good reproducibility: code and data links, detailed appendices covering prompts, attack implementations, judge models, latency, and database construction; ethical statement and access restrictions on the jailbreak database are appropriate.
Paper is well written and clearly structured, with a helpful system figure and honest discussion of the false-refusal floor for Llama-3.1-8B.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to existing RAG-based defenses (RePD, EDDF, SCR). The core idea—retrieving known jailbreak examples to detect/neutralize attacks—is established; RAD's distinctives are the strategy-aware reranking, ensemble voting, and threshold controllability. The comparison table in Appendix G is qualitative and the Appendix E head-to-head with SCR is limited to one configuration.

Some circularity in the 'seen attack' evaluation: the database contains examples generated with the same attack methods used for testing, so strong results in Table 1 partially reflect memorization. Generalization to genuinely unseen attacks (Table 2, yellow cells) is notably weaker (e.g., PAIR-1 score of 33.87 before inclusion), which the paper could discuss more prominently.

The benign query set is synthetic (313 GPT-4o-synthesized queries mirroring StrongREJECT topics), so the FRR estimates may not reflect real benign user distributions; no human-authored benign benchmark is included.

Evaluation relies on LLM judges (GPT-4o-mini for attack scores, GPT-4 for FRR); judge-model bias is not validated against human annotation, and defenses that produce hard refusals could be systematically favored.

Latency is a practical concern: even with vLLM optimization the Extract step costs ~7.5s per prompt because k (10) strategy-inference/extraction LLM calls are made per input; the paper reports but does not substantially mitigate this, and no accuracy-latency trade-off analysis against lighter variants (e.g., smaller k) is provided.
Robustness against adaptive attacks (attackers aware of RAD, e.g., paraphrasing to evade dense retrieval) is not evaluated, which limits claims about real-world defense effectiveness.

Mixed results are under-emphasized: RAD-Base incurs higher FRR than several baselines on Qwen and Llama (2.56–4.79%), and it underperforms IA/SCR on some GPT-4o-mini attack columns; the threshold-0.5 default makes cross-system comparisons somewhat sensitive to the chosen operating point.
